name: Aaron Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. Your answers are confidential. What does a usual shift hold?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and answer calls and chats on the night rota at a contact centre. I finished secondary school and still need help with unusual returns, so I'm junior even though the shift premium pays well. I use an approved AI draft every day and open the receipt before I send an answer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who and what waits after the shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Rosa works at a florist. Our children are ten and fourteen, the mortgage is ongoing, and we have nine months of expenses saved. Several other centres are close by. My brother runs a glazing workshop, but I wouldn't expect him to give me a paid place just because we're family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the little drafting tool helps me find a return policy quicker. I still check the receipt before I tell a customer yes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel fairly safe at the centre. I'm junior and miss unusual exceptions, but the night rate pays well and Rosa and I have nine months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my night calls and use the approved AI draft each shift, checking it against the actual receipt. Through the first year I'll put some of the night premium back into savings after the roof bill we paid last spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job. I still want to get better at the rules, but the mortgage is covered while both wages come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who depends on this pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa works at a florist, and our children are ten and fourteen. We saved the reserve slowly. Home repairs never announce themselves politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the draft fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The draft once said a stained tablecloth could be returned after use. I found the exception on the receipt and caught it before sending a wrong promise.

say: I'd say **AI drafts** can find a return rule faster.
I'd still check the **receipt exception** before promising money.
think: I feel **secure** with night pay and nine months saved.
I still need to learn **unusual returns** before I can trust my own speed.
do: Keep taking **night calls** through the first year.
Check each **AI draft** against the receipt and policy.
Restore **roof-repair savings** from the night premium when paid.
S0.quote: Home repairs never announce themselves politely.
fieldNote: His **night premium** explains higher pay despite junior standing.
He uses **AI daily** but checks a physical receipt before promising a return.
The **nine-month reserve** was built through steady household saving.

steps.text: Keep answering night calls and checking AI drafts against receipts
Replace roof-repair savings from paid night premiums

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to test automated replies on real return exceptions before changing the rota. I want the machine's wrong promises counted as carefully as its fast replies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The simple night chats that give me practice could vanish, and the premium could follow them. We have nine months saved and several centres nearby, but that doesn't recreate our monthly wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare twenty returned-goods cases with the new reply system on paid time. If my night hours fall in the first year, I'll check posted paid shifts at two nearby centres and apply only if their hours and pay cover the mortgage and replace the premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I want to see the results myself. I won't quit a good wage over a demonstration screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks your test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a senior agent to check my twenty cases so I don't mistake my own error for the tool's. I would show the corrected count at the next team meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family work be a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother runs a small glazing workshop, but there is no spare wage there today. I would ask for a paid place only if one opens, not arrive expecting family to hire me.

say: I'd test **return exceptions** before the centre changes shifts, using real old cases rather than a polished demonstration.
I'd count **wrong promises** alongside faster replies.
think: I might lose my **night premium** when simple chats vanish.
I know **nine months saved** cannot replace a regular wage forever.
do: Compare **twenty return cases** with the new system on paid time.
Share **checked error counts** with the team and senior agent.
Apply for **posted paid centre shifts** after cuts only if hours and pay cover mortgage and premium.
feel: **Anxious** about lost premium, yet ready to test.
S1.quote: I won't quit a good wage over a demonstration screen.
fieldNote: He measures the tool by **false return promises**, not speed alone.
His **family workshop** has no current paid opening.
His **night premium** creates an earnings floor for any move.

steps.text: Compare twenty returned-goods cases with AI during paid time
Apply for posted paid centre shifts after cuts if pay and hours cover mortgage and premium

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues general AI by 2028 could handle the returns I am still learning. Robots around 2031 come later for hands-on jobs, but that is no extra time for our headsets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my night role could end, and other centres might buy the same system together. Nine months saved gives us a search window, not a new income for the mortgage and two children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll ask for written notice and put away the money I had set aside for a garden shed. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for a posted paid glazier trainee place at my brother's workshop only if one exists and its wage and hours cover our bills; I won't leave for unpaid family work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have choices, but the two-year clock is short enough to make them feel narrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rosa that the shed can wait and show her how long our reserve lasts at current spending. We would not promise the children a move until a wage is written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would glazing stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fitting windows is hands-on for now, but robots around 2031 could change that work too. I'd take a paid trial day and ask about the actual duties before calling it a second career.

say: I'd warn **2028 thinking AI** could take our calls.
I'd explain **2031 robots** do not delay call-centre cuts.
think: I expect my **night role** could disappear with nearby centres shrinking.
I know **nine months saved** cannot pay our mortgage indefinitely.
do: Request **written notice** and delay buying the shed now.
Apply for a **posted paid trainee place** only after a cut and if wages and hours cover bills.
Try a **paid glazing day** before treating the work as a new career.
feel: **Anxious** because a strong reserve still has an end.
S2.quote: Nine months saved gives us a search window, not a new income for the mortgage and two children.
fieldNote: He treats the **brother's workshop** as an employer that must offer a wage.
He postpones a **shed purchase** before spending the reserve.
He sees the **2031 robot risk** in glazing as well.

steps.text: Delay buying the planned garden shed now
Apply after job ends for posted paid glazing with bill-covering wage and hours
Refuse unpaid family glazing and keep paid work
Take paid glazing trial day and inspect actual duties before treating it as a career

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to learn which paid openings really exist. Our calls face general AI in 2031, before robots do hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could get quicker on unusual returns and test my brother's workshop without resigning. Even a paid glazing job might change when robots arrive, so I would not borrow to open a shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the night shift and practise one hard return with a senior agent each week. If my brother advertises a paid trainee opening whose hours and pay cover the mortgage, I'll try a paid day; in the first year after 2031 I'll take that work only if a written offer still meets those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but five years lets me look at the whole workday. A family name gets me a conversation, not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a trial show you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see the lifting, measuring and travel, not only the neat finished window. I will ask what tasks his crew still does by hand as 2034 approaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for training now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't buy a glazing qualification now. I'd enrol only if a posted paid place requires it and the fee fits outside our mortgage reserve.

say: I'd check **paid openings** during the five-year window.
I'd tell coworkers **2034 robots** follow our 2031 call risk.
think: I could improve on **hard returns** while still earning.
I won't borrow for **shop ownership** before testing paid glazing work.
do: Keep my **paid night shift** while it remains.
Practise **hard returns** weekly with a senior agent.
Try a **paid glazing day** only for a posted opening whose pay and hours cover mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy**, with time to see a real workday.
S3.quote: A family name gets me a conversation, not a pay packet.
fieldNote: He requires a **posted paid place** even at his brother's workshop.
His **current-job practice** keeps him on paid shifts.
He avoids a **shop loan** while the 2034 robot effect is unknown.

steps.text: Keep taking paid night calls and practising difficult returns
Try one paid glazing day only for a posted mortgage-covering opening
Move after 2031 only with written offer still covering mortgage with wage and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade lets parents make plans from real wages, not warnings alone. Thinking AI reaches calls in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 we may still owe on the mortgage, and I cannot promise the children will need nothing then. I can strengthen my return skills and check other work without leaving good night pay today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep the night shift and save part of each paid premium toward a full year of expenses. I'll check posted centre and glazing openings twice a year; in the first year after 2036 I'll move only if my hours fall and a written paid offer covers our mortgage with steady hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan. Ten years is a long time to test a few paths while our wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to ask about paid apprenticeships before buying a course. Skill grows beside someone who knows the work, not from a certificate alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you fund a larger reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rosa and I would keep our mortgage reserve separate from any training fund. If night premiums stop, the one-year target moves back with them.

say: I'd plan from **posted wages** and hours, not distant warnings that do not show what a family can earn.
I'd separate **2036 call work** from 2039 hands-on robots.
think: I may still owe a **mortgage at 53**.
I can build **return skills** while preserving good night pay.
do: Keep my **night shift** while it pays.
Save part of **paid premiums** toward a full year of expenses.
Move after 2036 only if **hours fall** and a written paid offer has steady hours and mortgage-covering wages.
feel: **Calm** with a decade to test paid routes.
S4.quote: Skill grows beside someone who knows the work, not from a certificate alone.
fieldNote: His **one-year target** depends on continuing night premiums.
He values **paid apprenticeship** more than a speculative certificate.
His **mortgage reserve** stays separate from potential training spending.

steps.text: Keep taking paid night calls while the shift remains
Save paid night premiums toward one year of household expenses
Move after 2036 only if hours fall and written paid offer covers mortgage with steady hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The centre might lose night calls before I master hard returns, and nearby centres could cut too. Written notice and a posted paid opening with mortgage-covering hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays when a wrong return promise goes out. A customer still needs someone to own a mistake, even if the answer was drafted by a system. I'd rather see a named person than a blank help page.

headlineQuote: A customer still needs someone to own a mistake, even if the answer was drafted by a system.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old junior agent** with secondary schooling who still needs help on unusual returns.
A **night premium** gives him higher pay, and the family has nine months saved alongside a mortgage and two school-age children.
He uses **AI daily** and checks it against receipts; many other contact centres are nearby.
His brother's **glazing workshop** is a possible paid route, though Aaron insists on a posted place and sees later robot risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his night calls before he masters harder work.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** would show when the night wage might end.
A **posted paid place** with mortgage-covering hours would permit a measured move.
